When used in GLP studies for data generation relevant to device‐related pathologic findings, and thus for data interpretation, gross photographs are considered to be pathology raw data and need to be appropriately annotated (labeled), described (using detailed figure legends to explain key features of the tissue response), and archived. [ , , , ] In many cases, gross examination of the implant site and associated tissue responses needs to be delayed until tissue trimming to ensure that preparation of specimens for microscopic evaluation does not produce potentially confounding artifacts (see Section above); in such instances, additional photographic documentation at tissue trimming can aid the pathologist in defining potential regions of interest for microscopic evaluation, defining features to examine and possible scoring criteria to use in the microscopic evaluation, and to identify handling artifacts that should not be attributed to the implanted device. In general, the need for multiple stages of photographic documentation should be identified well in advance of necropsy, preferably during protocol development. For the macroscopic pathology evaluation (whether at necropsy on unfixed tissues or at tissue trimming for fixed tissues, or both), comments that provide context for specific diagnoses in various photographs and, in many cases, the photographs themselves (usually as well‐annotated “representative” depictions of key findings) should be incorporated as part of the pathology report. These macroscopic observations may need to be correlated with microscopic findings, particularly for studies conducted under GLP. For microscopic evaluation, the collection, annotation, and reporting of photographic data from all tissues, even normal tissues, for some or all animals in a medical device study (i.e., “exhaustive photographic documentation”) is an expensive and time‐consuming process for sponsors and pathologists. Comprehensive photographic documentation typically adds dozens or hundreds of images that should be well‐annotated and must be archived as pathology raw data. This type of exhaustive documentation for a nonclinical study seldom, if ever, adds value (especially for minimally annotated images) since correct interpretation of biological responses in response to implanted devices requires a substantial degree of tissue‐specific anatomy and cytology knowledge that is rarely attainable without dedicated advanced study of pathology. Moreover, exhaustive documentation is not consistent with the spirit of the “least burdensome” provisions (defined as “the minimum amount of information necessary to adequately address a relevant regulatory question or issue through the most efficient manner at the right time”) as promulgated by the FDA. [ ] Instead, for GLP‐compliant studies, the “representative illustration” approach for depicting tissue responses where the most common findings are photographed and characterized by detailed annotations and descriptions is the currently accepted pathology best practice for documenting microscopic findings for other biomedical product classes ( Figure ). [ ] In this approach, appropriate descriptions of key findings are included in the report narrative and/or figure legends, and by design such explanatory text better ensures the accuracy and interpretability of pathology raw data compared to exhaustive photographic documentation with little or no labeling and limited interpretative discussion. Representative photographs prepared and annotated by the study pathologist are generally used for informational and communication purposes rather than as a substitute for microscopic evaluation when making primary morphological diagnoses of tissue sections. Importantly, unusual “non‐representative” findings that inform the interpretation may also be photographed and annotated at the pathologist's discretion to provide a more nuanced assessment of the tissue response. In general, this “representative illustration” approach should be adopted for medical device studies as it is designed to provide a data set of the highest value at the least cost in terms of labor and time. In contrast, exhaustive photographic documentation is a futile endeavor that should be avoided in data generation for nonclinical studies of medical devices and combination products. Despite recent integration of digital whole slide imaging (WSI) into the GLP pathology workflow, digital images are not typically used (yet) for primary diagnoses of biological responses, [ , , ] although some companies are investigating their ability to replace evaluation of glass slides with WSI. A potential advantage of such digitized images is that they are amenable to automated or semi‐automated quantitative analyses such as cell counts, morphometry, or stereology (as discussed under Section below). When incorporated into pathology reports, portions of WSI should be annotated appropriately in the same fashion as conventional photomicrographs of tissue sections. Pathology data capture systems that are validated in compliance with CFR Part 11 (which covers appropriate use of electronic records [ ] ) or non‐validated but well‐organized tabulation systems (e.g., Microsoft ® Excel spreadsheets with pivot tables, Word tables) are generally used for pathology data capture during medical device studies. Non‐validated data recording does not adhere to GLP (and thus results in a

semi‐automated quantitative analyses such as cell counts, morphometry, or stereology (as discussed under Section below). When incorporated into pathology reports, portions of WSI should be annotated appropriately in the same fashion as conventional photomicrographs of tissue sections. Pathology data capture systems that are validated in compliance with CFR Part 11 (which covers appropriate use of electronic records [ ] ) or non‐validated but well‐organized tabulation systems (e.g., Microsoft ® Excel spreadsheets with pivot tables, Word tables) are generally used for pathology data capture during medical device studies. Non‐validated data recording does not adhere to GLP (and thus results in a GLP exception), but such data tables are audited for accuracy and thus are still suitable for interpretation. Similarly, other sources of imaging, such as standard radiography, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), may not be compliant with CFR Part 11. Thus, imaging technology that cannot be fully validated and is necessary for data generation should be audited and described as an exception in the GLP Compliance Statement for the study. In summary, toxicologic pathologists know by long experience in testing biomedical products that selective photographic documentation of representative tissue findings (with appropriate annotation) to supplement rather than supplant appropriately detailed pathology descriptions is both easier and more informative than the box‐checking enterprise of exhaustive photographic documentation with limited or no annotation that is the typical expectation for conventional medical device studies. Unfortunately, until this evidence‐based perspective used in drug testing is also adopted for evaluating medical devices, sponsors and regulatory agencies may continue to request a more burdensome approach of supplying exhaustive photographs as appendices to detailed medical device reports that already incorporate well‐chosen and effectively annotated representative images. Nonetheless, a detailed narrative description characterizing key tissue responses supplemented by a limited number of well‐annotated representative images of key tissue responses for a carefully selected subset of samples to depict those tissue responses is superior in terms of both value and resource utilization (compared to exhaustive photographic documentation) in understanding the principal features of the tissue response to a given medical device. The use of representative photographic documentation (gross and/or microscopic), undertaken on a case‐by‐case basis at the discretion of the study pathologist, is generally sufficient to demonstrate relevant pathology findings, provide macroscopic spatial context for the device and anatomic site, and/or document relative biological response scores for principal microscopic findings within a study. 6.2 Tissue Evaluations and Scoring a Biological Response No one‐size‐fits‐all study design is available for microscopic evaluation of implanted medical devices and combination products. Instead, pathology analysis is based on detailed knowledge of local, regional, and systemic anatomy relevant to the implant location; species variations; and consideration of the biomaterial type, its intended activity, and the clinical indication for the device. Implant study design with respect to the pathology evaluation must be tailored to answer specific questions regarding safety (including biocompatibility) and sometimes functional performance. [ ] Semi‐quantitative scoring to achieve the intended objectives as stated in ISO 10993–6:2016 (local) and ISO 10993‐11:2017 (systemic) evaluation needs to be flexible so that pathology endpoints may be targeted to the device and specific anatomic and physiological characteristics of the implant site(s). The biological evaluation and scoring recommendations provided in ISO 10993–6:2016, Annex E are general (inherently broad), so these example scoring systems are neither optimized nor validated for most tissues. Moreover, these general points are intended to be informative and not prescriptive. Therefore, strict implementation of such example scoring rubrics and calculations may result in inaccurate and/or uninterpretable pathology data leading to an inability to identify the existence and extent of biologically consequential tissue changes. In general, a conclusive determination of relative local tissue reactivity (test device compared to relevant control[s]) using only the simple mathematical calculations presented in ISO 10993–6:2016, Annex E does not work for some local implants (e.g., see intraocular implant example in Section and Table ), and indeed cannot effectively assess the complicated biological responses associated with many complex medical devices, combination products, or devices with surface or immunomodulator modifications. Quantitative evaluation of tissue responses may be helpful in some circumstances. In our experience, quantitative analysis for medical devices involves digital analysis of object numbers (e.g., cell counts, stereology) or dimensions (morphometry), but such methods can be applied reliably only with prior planning with respect to how to adequately and uniformly sample the specimen and mitigate for potential tissue collection and processing artifacts. [ , , ] While artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applied to digital image analysis may eventually streamline the planning needed to ensure appropriate tissue sampling and quantitative tissue analysis, validation and infrastructure issues with respect to maintaining vast quantities of electronic data will need to be addressed prior to widespread implementation of AI‐based methods for routine analysis of device‐related tissue responses. With respect to the emerging

but such methods can be applied reliably only with prior planning with respect to how to adequately and uniformly sample the specimen and mitigate for potential tissue collection and processing artifacts. [ , , ] While artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applied to digital image analysis may eventually streamline the planning needed to ensure appropriate tissue sampling and quantitative tissue analysis, validation and infrastructure issues with respect to maintaining vast quantities of electronic data will need to be addressed prior to widespread implementation of AI‐based methods for routine analysis of device‐related tissue responses. With respect to the emerging field of combination products where all elements of the regulated therapeutic candidate (drug/device, biologic/device, or drug/device/biologic) must be assessed for potential toxicity or other risks, [ ] we advise that the same rigorous terminology, biological criteria for diagnosing and interpreting tissue responses, and principles for assigning adversity and performing risk assessment should be used to evaluate device‐led, drug‐led, and biologic‐led combination products. In practice, current ISO 10993 standards for biological evaluation of medical devices are not consistent with expectations for drug‐based determinations of toxicity, let alone capable of efficiently and effectively addressing such expectations for combination products. Fortunately, the established guidelines and toxicologic pathology best practices for evaluating drugs are also readily adaptable to evaluating the medical device components of combination products, so defaulting to or adapting the drug‐based approach to any combination product is generally favored by toxicologic pathologists tasked with assessing tissue responses to implanted devices and combination products. Furthermore, the scoring system examples in ISO 10993–6:2016, Annex E seldom, if ever, are appropriate templates for use in assessing systemic responses to implants under ISO 10993‐11:2017, especially in terms of evaluating combination products. Development of a relevant scoring rubric with inclusion of a full interpretive narrative is necessary to effectively communicate the toxicological (“biological”) impact of therapeutics (drugs or medical devices) on whole body systems. In the authors’ experience, scoring systems frequently need to be created de novo and refined to some degree by the pathologist over the entire development lifespan of a medical device. Numerous recent publications provide recommendations for tissue‐ or device‐specific evaluation approaches to devising such scoring schemes. [ , , , , , , ] 6.2.1 Avoid Routine Use of Masked (“Blinded”) Histopathological Evaluation The benefits and pitfalls of masked (“blinded”) pathology evaluation have been discussed in several publications related to the practice of toxicologic pathology as applied to nonclinical studies. Although an initial masked analysis is sometimes useful to control observer bias in a research setting, selection of masked microscopic evaluation as a routine approach to assessing tissue responses is not aligned with current best practices for data generation in toxicologic pathology, and in fact can render a pathology data set uninterpretable. [ ] Therefore, the initial pathology evaluation generally should be an informed (“non‐blinded”) analysis rather than a masked assessment. [ ] Masked pathology evaluation is warranted in some situations. For example, masked evaluation is suitable for testing specific hypotheses and discriminating whether potential pathology findings identified during an initial informed assessment are genuine. However, routine masking of the pathologist has limited benefit and, in fact is often detrimental when seeking to understand the true nature of a tissue response when assessing safety and potential human relevance. Masked evaluation adds time and cost to the biological response evaluation, for several reasons. First, discriminating the range of background/spontaneous changes from treatment‐related findings is time‐consuming at best and may be impossible. Second, masked evaluation will substantially delay the study timeline since data analysis and interpretation must wait until the data are unmasked. Finally, masked microscopic evaluation typically results in an abundance of findings, many of which are not related to the test device, as the pathologist tends to over‐diagnose in order to “not miss anything”;* excessive diagnoses increase the “noise” (incidental findings and artifacts) and obscure the “signal” of interest (genuine test device‐related tissue responses). This issue is especially common for early studies when the pathologist is first starting to work with a unique device, and may be problematic since it is not uncommon to have only one small pilot study prior to launching a GLP study to enable a regulatory submission to support clinical testing. The optimal analytical approach for pathology analysis is an informed evaluation in which the toxicologic pathologist has awareness of all information, including the device identity, when performing their examination. Providing the pathologist with information regarding the study materials typically expedites tissue evaluation and report preparation without introducing unacceptable bias or compromising data generation and interpretation. [ ] An informed evaluation generally provides a more accurate and credible pathology data set as the improved signal‐to‐noise ratio better supports identification of potential treatment‐related changes. Importantly, many devices can only be evaluated in an “informed” fashion since masking is impossible (even

clinical testing. The optimal analytical approach for pathology analysis is an informed evaluation in which the toxicologic pathologist has awareness of all information, including the device identity, when performing their examination. Providing the pathologist with information regarding the study materials typically expedites tissue evaluation and report preparation without introducing unacceptable bias or compromising data generation and interpretation. [ ] An informed evaluation generally provides a more accurate and credible pathology data set as the improved signal‐to‐noise ratio better supports identification of potential treatment‐related changes. Importantly, many devices can only be evaluated in an “informed” fashion since masking is impossible (even with time‐intensive efforts) due to their unique identifying characteristics, which can be seen readily in tissue sections. The frequent use of a single test group in medical device studies obviates the need for masking. When a masked evaluation is performed, current best practice states that the only information to be withheld from the pathologist is information regarding the treatment (e.g., test device vs. positive control device vs. other control). [ ] 6.2.2 Pathology Peer Review is a Cost‐ and Time‐Effective Replacement for Exhaustive Photographic Documentation of Macroscopic and/or Microscopic Findings As is the current practice for drugs, a superior and substantially less burdensome approach for documenting tissue responses in medical device studies would be to incorporate proper study design, adhere to GLP principles (where possible), select an experienced and qualified pathologist for the evaluation, [ ] and undertake a peer review of the pathology data. [ , , , , ] Pathology peer review procedures are an established feature of nonclinical drug development to ensure the quality of pathology data, [ , ] which are widely recognized as adding substantial value to nonclinical studies by the FDA [ ] and other global regulatory authorities. [ , ] Existing peer review procedures are already being adapted for and incorporated into medical device studies by toxicologic pathologists. Pathology peer review of the preliminary diagnoses and interpretations of one pathologist (the “study pathologist”) by a second individual (the “peer review pathologist”) is designed to ensure the accuracy and consistency (credibility) of research data that are, by their essential nature, subject to some degree of subjectivity in their acquisition. Pathology peer reviews by independent third parties, rather than “in house” peer reviews, are preferred for GLP studies. At present, peer reviews need not be performed at GLP‐compliant test sites since their function is a quality check rather than the generation of pathology raw data. [ ] The GLP character of the data is maintained by ensuring that the original evaluation by the study pathologist is performed in a GLP‐compliant setting subject to a suitable quality assurance (QA) audit. Pathology peer reviews should always be undertaken as an informed evaluation since their purpose is to check the quality of the initial assessment. [ ] If necessary, a pathology working group (PWG) composed of multiple experienced pathologists may be undertaken to adjudicate differences between the study pathologist and peer review pathologist and to reach a diagnostic consensus for any contentious findings. [ , , ] Such PWGs are employed most frequently for unusual tumors in carcinogenicity bioassays but may be assembled if warranted for other unusual tissue responses and thus could conceivably be used when warranted for medical device studies. Pathology peer review typically requires examination of a selected subset of prepared tissue sections by the peer review pathologist, including all tissues from at least 10% of randomly selected test and control animals and all target organs or lesions from all test and control animals. [ ] White papers highlighting key “Points to Consider” concepts are also available for digital pathology peer review. [ ] Along with examination of the tissue sections and opportunity for the peer review pathologist to request all supporting data and documentation (for in vivo clinical observations, clinical pathology, necropsy, histology and histopathology phases of the study), peer review by an independent pathologist situated outside of a primary testing CRO ensures the quality of the pathology (gross and microscopic) data with respect to the terminology, morphological diagnoses, severity scoring, and biological response interpretation. Importantly, peer review under GLP provides confirmation of adequate protocol tissue availability for histopathology evaluation and interpretation [ ] and that tissues presented for peer review were actually collected from appropriate test animals. Oversight of the pathology components of the medical device testing program by a GLP‐trained and experienced toxicologic pathologist, and peer review of the preliminary pathology diagnoses by a similarly qualified and independent toxicologic pathologist, is a far superior method to exhaustive photographic documentation to ensure the credibility of pathology data and that scientifically accurate interpretation has occurred. This concept is particularly important in light of the 20 February 2024 FDA Letter to Industry warning about fraudulent third‐party testing on medical devices. [ ] 6.3 Considerations for

and that tissues presented for peer review were actually collected from appropriate test animals. Oversight of the pathology components of the medical device testing program by a GLP‐trained and experienced toxicologic pathologist, and peer review of the preliminary pathology diagnoses by a similarly qualified and independent toxicologic pathologist, is a far superior method to exhaustive photographic documentation to ensure the credibility of pathology data and that scientifically accurate interpretation has occurred. This concept is particularly important in light of the 20 February 2024 FDA Letter to Industry warning about fraudulent third‐party testing on medical devices. [ ] 6.3 Considerations for Determination of Complete Bioabsorption Identification of medical device degradation or bioabsorption and its impact (or lack thereof) on tissues is not well‐described in standards and guidance documents. Nonetheless, staging the extent of degradation and determining the degree of bioabsorption is an oft‐requested endpoint by regulatory reviewers. [ ] A state‐of‐the‐art description of the immunological and tissue responses to different medical devices and the complete early bioabsorption through reparative processes is beyond the scope of this publication. We could not identify an extant comprehensive review that properly reflects the current understanding and variation in biological responses to different biomaterials that would help to define bioabsorption, which generally needs to be determined on a case‐by‐case basis. Therefore, inclusion of a preformulated scoring rubric to estimate bioabsorption and residual biomaterials in tissues would suffer from the same scientific fallacies and prospects for misapplication that occur with the suggested scoring rubrics in Annex E of ISO 10993–6:2016. Complete bioabsorption may or may not occur depending on such factors as the implant material, type and activity of the device, and implant location. Trace amounts of sequestered (residual) biomaterial and immune cells in the tissue near implantation sites may occur in situations featuring physiologically complete bioabsorption and restoration of tissue integrity ( Figure ). Certain implants can leave end‐of‐process biomaterial trace deposits such as fragmented or mineralized debris sequestered within macrophages or multinucleated giant cells, encompassed by a fibrous capsule or matrix, or trapped within bone trabeculae; such residues may be accompanied by persistent accumulation of long‐lived immune sentinel cells, including lymphocytes, macrophages, and/or multinucleated giant cells. The pathologist may judge these trace deposits and cell aggregates as innocuous and consistent with completion of the bioabsorptive process at the implantation site. Residuals present in trace amounts (i.e., rare or barely perceptible) observed within a tissue that has reached a “steady state” of repair and regeneration (where “steady state” as applied to the tissue response indicates either restoration or at least no further progression) as well as residuals that are passive bystanders that do not interfere with tissue healing or restoration of structural integrity can be interpreted to be within the physiologically expected anatomic limits (“normal”) expected of a dynamic tissue and serve as evidence that the bioabsorptive process has been completed. 7 Limitations of Toxicologic Pathology in Medical Device Evaluation Macroscopic and microscopic evaluation of tissue changes and differentiation between normal and abnormal tissue organization are qualitative or semi‐quantitative assessments where the resulting data rely heavily on the experience and informed professional judgment of the observer. [ ] A well‐designed study with clear objectives and well‐planned controls, appropriate collection and processing of tissues, selective photographic documentation, and where warranted pathology peer review provides the appropriate path to maximizing the scientific veracity of the biological response evaluation. Macroscopic pathology evaluations cannot identify all changes associated with a medical device, particularly if the device is large or has been bioabsorbed. Therefore, closer macroscopic observation is often best performed not at necropsy but when fine trimming and additional photographic documentation are undertaken during histology specimen preparation. Biotribology forces (i.e., interactions influenced by friction and fluctuating lubrication) can lead to fracture, wear, loosening, and/or failure of medical devices that may be difficult to confirm by macroscopic or microscopic examination in animal studies. Explantation of the device to test for post‐implantation function or failure may disrupt surrounding tissue and destroy some, if not all, of the tissue:implant interface, which may complicate interpretation. Regardless, postmortem determination of device failure is an important evaluation that will be best served by extensive planning and collaboration between the development team and the study pathologist. [ , , ] Failure testing includes a review of all engineering, in vitro, and in vivo efficacy and safety data as well as imaging and pathology data to make the final determination regarding whether device function has been altered and/or partial or complete device failure has occurred. Despite this need for data integration across scientific disciplines, we are not aware of Design Failure Mode and Effect Analysis approaches that incorporate pathology analysis endpoints. Similarly, the 2D anatomic representation of tissues available in flat tissue sections mounted on glass slides or digital images of such sections cannot identify functional changes in

, , ] Failure testing includes a review of all engineering, in vitro, and in vivo efficacy and safety data as well as imaging and pathology data to make the final determination regarding whether device function has been altered and/or partial or complete device failure has occurred. Despite this need for data integration across scientific disciplines, we are not aware of Design Failure Mode and Effect Analysis approaches that incorporate pathology analysis endpoints. Similarly, the 2D anatomic representation of tissues available in flat tissue sections mounted on glass slides or digital images of such sections cannot identify functional changes in cells or organs. However, histopathologic (microscopic) evaluation usually allows inferences to be made on potential functional changes and their degree of adversity (harm [ ] caused to the individual bearing the implant). In‐life observations and clinical pathology findings may also provide evidence of functional changes that can sometimes be correlated with tissue changes. For certain implantation sites, periodic in vivo imaging and/or postmortem micro‐computed tomography (µ‐CT) prior to tissue trimming can also help correlate tissue responses to functional changes or device failure. These correlations and their interpretations should be described in the pathology report narrative and (where warranted) may be included in the pathology data tables. Correlations (or lack thereof) and identification of potential adversity based on in vivo and postmortem examinations are important components of the nonclinical risk assessment. 7.1 Why Biological Evaluation of Tissue Responses in Animal Studies Can Fail Poor communication among study participants may lead to poor study designs, resulting in insufficient or inappropriate sampling for analytical analysis and histological evaluation, many times as a result of competing endpoints between bioengineering and biological evaluation objectives. The study protocol should be assessed by all participants, including the pathologist responsible for evaluating the biological responses, before finalization to confirm that the correct or important questions are being asked, that the entire plan is feasible, and to assess whether multiple studies will be needed to meet all program objectives. Any major variance from the regulatory guidance with respect to GLP compliance, study design features, and analytical approach should be discussed in advance with the regulatory agencies, if possible, and documented (along with the scientific justification for the variance) in protocol amendments and the final reports. 8 Concluding Perspectives Pathology evaluations are a substantive, and perhaps the most critical component in biological assessments regarding the safety, efficacy, and risk of many Class II and Class III medical devices and combination products prior to clinical use. The advent of increasingly complex medical devices, longer contact time in patients, recognition of potential systemic impacts of medical devices, and increasing use of combination products incorporating a device component with a bioactive substance have increased the importance of clearly identifying the range of tissue reactions, and especially adverse findings, that may be incited by implanted medical devices. Toxicologic pathologists who specialize in nonclinical evaluation of implanted medical devices play a critical role in supporting medical device development, especially for devices that require a nonclinical study to investigate implant biocompatibility and safety. Historical differences in the development of medical devices versus drugs as well as disparate training backgrounds among engineers, materials scientists, pathologists, toxicologists, and regulatory scientists have resulted in different perspectives regarding appropriate and necessary elements of nonclinical study designs for medical devices. Divergent perspectives regarding the desired study objectives, feasible and reliable endpoints for evaluating biological responses, acceptable diagnostic nomenclature, and data interpretation and reporting conventions for pathology endpoints may substantially complicate translation of animal data to assess potential patient risk. In this paper, we have emphasized that the toxicologic pathology literature increasingly provides resources that are important not only to medical device pathologists but also to other stakeholders (e.g., bioengineers, materials scientists, toxicologists, and regulatory reviewers) seeking experienced counsel regarding suitable approaches to evaluating biological responses to medical devices and combination products. Engagement of a knowledgeable and experienced toxicologic pathologist should be a routine practice to align the tissue analysis in a study protocol with general principles found in guidance documents (e.g., by FDA and ISO) and published expert recommendations on biological response evaluation (mainly white papers prepared by working groups of the Society of Toxicologic Pathology [STP]) and European Society of Toxicologic Pathology [ESTP]). Indeed, such engagement is often a critical first step to determine optimal approaches to tissue collection, data generation and documentation (descriptive text and photographic depictions), and scoring systems relevant to the species and medical device (with respect to type, composition, and implantation site), thereby ensuring that data are accurate and interpretability is clear for a medical device study. In addition, the development of combination products requires understanding and implementation of many additional guidance documents and standards from multiple agencies relevant to drug development. Again, toxicologic pathologists are intimately acquainted with the contents of such drug‐related commentaries, and

Toxicologic Pathology [ESTP]). Indeed, such engagement is often a critical first step to determine optimal approaches to tissue collection, data generation and documentation (descriptive text and photographic depictions), and scoring systems relevant to the species and medical device (with respect to type, composition, and implantation site), thereby ensuring that data are accurate and interpretability is clear for a medical device study. In addition, the development of combination products requires understanding and implementation of many additional guidance documents and standards from multiple agencies relevant to drug development. Again, toxicologic pathologists are intimately acquainted with the contents of such drug‐related commentaries, and in particular the optimal means of integrating their precepts with those needed for biological evaluation of medical devices. In conclusion, expert perspectives of experienced toxicologic pathologists should be incorporated automatically in each nonclinical study protocol that assesses a medical device or combination product. A protocol allowing appropriate flexibility to the biological response evaluation (in establishing features to be scored as well as relevant scoring criteria) will yield satisfactory results more consistently than will strict adherence only to the inflexible and generic example scoring rubrics enshrined in current guidance documents and ISO standards. Such flexibility will also offer additional benefits, including lower cost and more rapid evaluation because common pathology practices can be applied more quickly and reproducibly with substantially less labor compared to the multiple parameters in the ISO 10993–6:2016, Annex E scoring examples. [ ] Moreover, our collective experience in assessing medical device safety has shown that utilizing simplistic example rubrics often significantly handicaps pathology data generation and interpretation, resulting in inappropriate adversity determinations and skewed or useless risk assessments. In principle, following well‐established industrial practices for effective pathology evaluation [ ] to capture and communicate scientifically accurate findings during nonclinical studies is as applicable to medical devices and combination products as it is to other biomedical products. Furthermore, extension of these established pathology principles to medical device studies would only require modest modifications to account for the variations in medical devices and differences in study objectives, application of data collection procedures specific to medical device categories and implantation sites, and awareness of potential unique terminology requirements. Such modest modifications would yield out‐sized benefits in terms of data reliability and reproducibility while also making interpretation, and thus regulatory decision‐making, easier. Importantly, toxicologic pathologists also understand the limitations of the conventional pathology evaluation process, including when and where scoring rubrics similar to the examples in ISO 10993–6:2016, Annex E may be used and when they should be spurned. Going forward, the authors strongly recommend that medical device studies increase the extent to which toxicologic pathology expertise is incorporated into study design and execution. Routine implementation of pathology “best practice” principles will provide a more rational decision‐making process for innovators and regulatory agencies developing medical materials and protecting human health, respectively. chunks.content: Introduction Low-resource settings (LRS), which can exist in countries of any income level, are often thought of as communities where constraints on finances, health literacy, medical infrastructure and delivery, or social and human resources contribute to inequities of and limit the potential for optimal health outcomes [ ]. Congruently, children living in LRS face a disproportionately high burden of treatable deaths, infections, and malnutrition along with a rising incidence of non-communicable diseases [ ]. Clinically and contextually appropriate medical equipment and technologies are critical tools used by healthcare providers to address these challenges [ ]. However, many products targeting the pediatric population fail to sustainably scale due to poorly defined pathways for development and commercialization, especially in LRS [ , ]. The barriers to designing and marketing medical technologies for children are multifactorial, and include a small market size, a wide range of rapid changes in anatomy and physiology, and the legal and ethical mandates surrounding testing products for children – and these challenges are magnified in LRS [ – ]. Lack of consistent electricity is a common problem faced and can render many types of equipment unreliable or even dangerous to use with children. Furthermore, implementing and maintaining service contracts for imported devices are nearly impossible to honor, leading to abandoned equipment when malfunctions occur [ ]. In addition, it can be difficult for national regulatory systems to engage international stakeholders who are beholden to external standards. Designing devices and tools specifically for LRS, focusing on maximizing accessibility and sustainability, may overcome potential barriers. One such approach is to utilize the “open-source” process, a concept first used by computer software developers in the 1950s [ ]. Here, designs and manufacturing procedures are shared openly, typically on an online platform, from which any qualified operator can freely make, modify, or distribute a product tailored to a specific population. A common example is shared 3D printing instructions, though open-source work extends far beyond this. Open-source approach to medical technology dissemination covers the complete range of tasks required to build and distribute, including making the following freely available: the underlying design files, schematics, and/or assembly instructions. The goal is to promote transparency, adaptability, and local empowerment, rather than dependence on closed proprietary systems. In this way, such devices can be constructed or created in the communities or hospitals that live and work in LRS, thereby bypassing the financial and resource strains that foreign involvement often entail. For example, repairs and replacements of open-source devices can more often be done locally and without specialized or expensive assistance, as opposed to more expensive equipment imported overseas. Abiding by the obligations of foreign stakeholders may no longer be needed given that the open-source procedures, by definition, allow for local production and modification of such devices to fit the needs of local regulations. The open-source approach has created a pathway by which technologies have been tailored to ever-growing needs in LRS. Medical technologies thus far developed via open-source include non-invasive respiratory support targeting LRS in Nigeria, Cambodia, Mozambique, and Bangladesh [ – ]. In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, emergency mechanical ventilators [ , ] and hand hygiene and isolation gown sanitizer projects [ – ]. Taken together, open-source pathways may lead to improved cost of production, decentralization of supplies and expertise, and customizability in a way that facilitates pediatric technology innovation for austere settings and LRS [ – ]. Given the novelty of this approach, it is critical to assess the perspectives and attitudes held by healthcare providers who frequently work in technology-heavy medical sectors (i.e., intensive care) and/or LRS in order to craft impactful interventions. Therefore, in this descriptive study we sought to survey the perspectives and opinions of medical professionals on the viability of open-source applications for pediatric global health technology. Materials and Methods This exploratory study and questionnaire were approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board (IRB) (Protocol number 2022P002692) and built in compliance with SQUIRE guidelines [ ]. The entire survey was developed by the authors, then critically appraised by three pediatric critical care and emergency physicians with experience in global health and low-cost medical devices. Suggested improvements included providing an introduction to the survey and the study and adding more clarifying questions (i.e., “Please list known open-source pediatric medical devices.”). The survey was then refined, edited, and ultimately approved by the respective scientific review committees of the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies (WFPICCS) and the Pediatric Acute Lung Injury and Sepsis Network (PALISI) (See Supplemental File “ Survey Creation Timeline”) – 2 academic groups that jointly represent global pediatric critical care efforts (see Supplemental Document “Survey Creation Timeline”). and adding more clarifying questions (i.e., “Please list known open-source pediatric medical devices.”). The survey was then refined, edited, and ultimately approved by the respective scientific review committees of the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies (WFPICCS) and the Pediatric Acute Lung Injury and Sepsis Network (PALISI) (See Supplemental File “ Survey Creation Timeline”) – 2 academic groups that jointly represent global pediatric critical care efforts (see Supplemental Document “Survey Creation Timeline”). WFPICCS is an international network of 52 national, international, and regional member societies that represent pediatric and neonatal critical care practitioners from Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, North America, and Oceania. PALISI is a network of research investigators involving over 90 pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) in the U.S. and Canada seeking to optimize the care of critically ill children. Critical care practitioners were selected as respondents due to their unique position of recognizing patient need, often navigating complex medical infrastructure including delivery systems, funding streams, and high-level use of medical equipment. Potential respondents received an email from WFPICCS or PALISI, which included a description of the survey and link to the survey housed on REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture). Reminder emails were sent at 4 and 8 weeks after the initial email. The survey was active for a total of 3 months, from March 6, 2023, to June 1, 2023. Survey questions included multiple choice, free text, Likert, and checkbox (with ‘Choose more than 1,’ options) formatting. Occupation options included “physician”, “nurse”, “advanced practice provider”, “respiratory specialist”, or “other”. Questions asking about locations (i.e., countries) and devices were free text. Questions asking about factors to consider when implementing open-source devices and barriers to implementation provided discrete answer choices but also provided an “other” option. Likert-style questions were used when asked about comfort, feasibility, and having ethical concerns regarding open-source technology implementation in LRS. Respondents were informed on the survey that no sensitive or identifying information would be collected in the survey other than the country of practice and that voluntary completion of the online survey would constitute implied consent. The questionnaire contained 17 questions that captured data on a respondent’s experience with and knowledge about open-source pediatric medical devices and opinions on the feasibility of utilizing the open-source approach. [Survey copy available in Supplement] Study data were collected and managed using REDCap hosted at Mass General Brigham [ , ]. REDCap is a secure, web-based software platform designed to support data capture for research studies, providing: 1) an intuitive interface for validated data capture; 2) audit trails for tracking data manipulation and export procedures; 3) automated export procedures for seamless data downloads to common statistical packages; and 4) procedures for data integration and interoperability with external sources. Statistical analysis, performed in REDCap, included descriptive analysis and calculations of proportions. Results A total of 148 surveys were at least partially completed by respondents, of which 47 were incomplete, resulting in 101 (68.2%) completed surveys. Only completed surveys were used in the analysis to ensure consistency across variables. Among the 101 completed surveys, 90 (89%) were completed by physicians and 87 (86%) by providers identified as pediatric critical care specialists. Fifty-five respondents (55%) practiced primarily in the United States of America (USA); and more than 1 provider responded from Brazil, the United Kingdom, India, Kuwait, Peru, and Argentina; and single providers responded each from 27 other countries. ( ) Most of the respondents felt “critical care” (n = 81, 80.2%) and “emergency medicine” (n = 66, 65.4%) would benefit the most from open-source devices ( ). Of note, “Nephrology” was not provided as a defined answer option but was added by two respondents in the “Other” category as a specialty that would benefit. Sixty-nine (68.3%) of the respondents work in high-income countries (HIC), and 32 (31.7%) work in a low- or middle-income country, as defined by the World Bank [ ]. Seventy-five (74.3%) reported no experience working in “pediatric global health”, but the remaining 26 (25.7%) reported working in “pediatric global health,” of whom 11 (10.9%) also had experience working with pediatric medical devices. Overall, 16 (15.8%) respondents had prior experience working with pediatric medical devices and only 7 (6.9%) reported being aware of an example of an open-source pediatric medical device. Of the 10 examples of open-source devices provided, 4 were general terms (“prosthetic limbs”, “bubble CPAP”, “PPE”, “PALS devices”), 4 were open-source devices or groups (i.e., NeoTree, Glia Project, PVP1 ventilator, Goodscope), and 2, while low-cost-oriented, were not open-source devices or groups (IMPALA continuous monitoring system, Layco Medical). “Device durability” (n = 58, 57%) and “local institutional need and interest” (n = 57, 56.4%) were identified as the most important factors for operationalizing a device in LRS, while “government involvement” was thought to be the least important (n = 16, 15.8%).

Of the 10 examples of open-source devices provided, 4 were general terms (“prosthetic limbs”, “bubble CPAP”, “PPE”, “PALS devices”), 4 were open-source devices or groups (i.e., NeoTree, Glia Project, PVP1 ventilator, Goodscope), and 2, while low-cost-oriented, were not open-source devices or groups (IMPALA continuous monitoring system, Layco Medical). “Device durability” (n = 58, 57%) and “local institutional need and interest” (n = 57, 56.4%) were identified as the most important factors for operationalizing a device in LRS, while “government involvement” was thought to be the least important (n = 16, 15.8%). A total of 22 (21.8%) respondents had previously participated in attempts to increase accessibility to pediatric medical devices and, among this subgroup, perceived the greatest barrier to be “lack of funding” (n = 16, 72.7%) followed by “lack of local technical expertise and support” (n = 12, 54.5%). Thirteen of these 22 (59%) respondents practiced outside of the USA. When comparing responses about implementation factors and barriers (e.g., ‘believing that device durability is a major factor’, and ‘lack of funding is a major barrier’), answers were similar between the subgroup with pediatric global health experience (n = 26) and the subgroup with device experience (n = 16). Also, of note, the subgroup with device experience marked “lack of local material supplies” as less important of a barrier and “regulatory or policy restrictions” as a greater barrier. depicts the results from the Likert scale questions. The majority agreed or strongly agreed that providing an open-source pediatric medical device to LRS is feasible (n = 74, 73.2%); that delivering devices to children is particularly difficult (n = 55, 54.4%); and that ethical concerns were not a factor (n = 59, 58.4%). More respondents were comfortable working with a team to take a device from conception to market versus respondents who were not comfortable (45 vs 26). Of note, among the 45 who were comfortable taking a device from conception to market in an LRS, only 17 (37.7%) of them practiced in the USA. In contrast, 26 indicated they “strongly disagree” or “disagree” with being comfortable in taking a device from conception to market in an LRS, with 21 (81%) identifying as working in the USA. When asked if the respondent had ethical concerns with bringing devices to LRS, no one from the USA agreed or strongly agreed, but 12 respondents from outside the USA agreed or strongly agreed. Discussion In this international survey of 101 providers from 34 countries, we sought to identify the opinions about and gaps in experience with open-source medical hardware development and distribution in LRS. Though the majority of collected responses were authored by critical care physicians without experience working with open-source devices in LRS, many respondents felt comfortable with successfully providing an open-source pediatric medical device to LRS. Among those who had experience with pediatric medical devices, most felt that lack of funding was the most significant barrier to successfully deploying technologies in LRS. Most respondents felt that local need assessment was one of the most important factors when considering increasing access to open-source devices in LRS. These sentiments are consistent with recent global health literature that has emphasized the importance of conducting local needs assessments in the context of global health initiatives, emphasizing decolonialization, refocusing on the needs of the country, and promoting local ownership of health initiatives [ – ]. Lack of funding was identified as a significant barrier to providing open-source devices, highlighting the need for investment in cost-effective strategies or mechanisms for implementation. Examples of such efforts include the national Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Pediatric Device Consortia Program, although there is no precedent for analogous efforts in LRS, to our knowledge [ ]. Extending a similar mechanism to LRS is needed. Our survey results demonstrate a discrepancy between experience and comfort in approaching open-source pediatric devices for LRS. Forty-five respondents (44.5%) felt comfortable in this endeavor; however, only 11 of these 45 respondents reported having experience with devices in LRS. There may be a mismatch of the expectations and reality of attempting to implement open-source technology in LRS. For example, perhaps some practitioners with limited experience in the regulatory and development processes that take place before, during, and after a device is deployed underestimate the associated challenges. It is notable that most respondents who were comfortable taking a device from conception to market were from outside the USA, suggesting that providers in target LRS countries are more motivated to advance much needed technologies. Regardless, education and training in device development, manufacturing, and distribution should be integrated into global health didactic programs, wherein, according to our survey results, ‘device durability’ and ‘local needs assessment’ should be core concepts. We found it interesting that most respondents with experience in “pediatric global health” were from

that take place before, during, and after a device is deployed underestimate the associated challenges. It is notable that most respondents who were comfortable taking a device from conception to market were from outside the USA, suggesting that providers in target LRS countries are more motivated to advance much needed technologies. Regardless, education and training in device development, manufacturing, and distribution should be integrated into global health didactic programs, wherein, according to our survey results, ‘device durability’ and ‘local needs assessment’ should be core concepts. We found it interesting that most respondents with experience in “pediatric global health” were from the USA, but most respondents with experience with pediatric medical devices were from outside the USA. In this survey, we realize that “pediatric global health” may be viewed differently, based on the location of practice. Therefore, though some providers may not have experience in what they may call “pediatric global health”, they may already work in a low-resource setting. This survey element may also reflect that the type of global health work typically pursued by USA-based critical care practitioners does not involve the use of medical devices. Our survey found that practitioners based in the USA had no ethical concerns with bringing devices to LRS. Conversely, the 15 respondents who agreed (i.e., had ethical concerns) were all from outside the USA. This discrepancy underscores what has been shown previously: that medical practitioners in high-resource countries (HIC) and LRS have differing opinions on what it means to achieve equity in global health practice [ ]. For example, HIC investigators studying the implementation of new technology in a LRS may disproportionately allocate credits (leadership, authorship, funding) to the HIC investigators in the process. The perspectives and needs of the leaders in the LRS may be overshadowed by the priorities of the HIC team, which may promote the use of economic or academic pressures to control or influence the LRS despite best intentions. Such divergence may reflect deeper historical or systemic asymmetries. Many LRS practitioners may remain acutely aware of legacies of colonialism and resource extraction, which can shape their concerns about dependency, exploitation, and inequitable benefit-sharing. In contrast, practitioners in HICs may be more insulated from these narratives. There is, therefore, an opportunity for shared learning and strategizing among partners for ways to minimize any ethical tension when approaching medical device distribution to LRS [ ]. Furthermore, it is important that individuals representing a local population independently support the development of the target technology in these partnerships. Of note, we did not include any queries in the survey to further delineate the interpretation of “ethical concerns”. Our study has a few noteworthy limitations. First, the survey was limited to mostly critical care practitioners through two critical care networks. New technologies can certainly be applied by providers from other specialties or with specific research backgrounds (which was not asked) and should be explored in future investigations. While WFPICCS and PALISI are considered among the largest networks of pediatric critical care providers in the world, future investigations should be sent outside of these two organizations to better capture the full breadth of providers in LRS (membership to said societies often requires resources – internet access and funding – to participate). Future related work may also consider surveying the perspectives of professionals outside the critical care specialty, professionals who are more frequently at bedside (i.e., nurses), or those who work with other aspects of device development, such as engineers or public health workers, who may have additional insight into other aspects of device implementation. Indeed, the fact that a minority of respondents were aware of any open-source devices highlights that additional information is needed to more accurately capture information on how open-source approaches are viewed by relevant professions. Additionally, despite an attempt to capture a global audience, almost half of the respondents practiced in the USA and two-thirds of respondents who had experience in global health are based in the USA. This potentially reflects the current geographic distribution of pediatric critical care providers in the world [ ]. However, determination of this in our study is limited by our low response rate. This may have been due to a lack of interest or familiarity with the topic. Indeed, no previous studies or evaluations have been published documenting the lack of open-resource devices in LRS – only that interest is growing despite multiple barriers to these efforts. Our survey reflects this gap given that most respondents did not have experience working either in pediatric global health or with open-source medical devices in LRS, which may limit how some of these results may be interpreted. For example, most respondents agreed that assessing the local need is crucial to implementing such technology, but it may not be an accurate sentiment if it reflects opinions of those with little

the topic. Indeed, no previous studies or evaluations have been published documenting the lack of open-resource devices in LRS – only that interest is growing despite multiple barriers to these efforts. Our survey reflects this gap given that most respondents did not have experience working either in pediatric global health or with open-source medical devices in LRS, which may limit how some of these results may be interpreted. For example, most respondents agreed that assessing the local need is crucial to implementing such technology, but it may not be an accurate sentiment if it reflects opinions of those with little experience. Relatedly, given the potential variability in how participants perceived the meaning of “global health” or “pediatric medical device”, future work should involve a guiding definition of both terms to ensure consistent understanding among the respondents regardless of geography or medical scope. Lastly, our survey was only provided in English. Conclusion According to this exploratory study comprised of responses largely representing critical care providers in high-resource settings, most pediatric practitioners worldwide are unaware of or lack experience with open-source pediatric medical devices in LRS, with significant geographic variability. Our results reflect a disparity that magnifies the disconnect between provides in LRS and those in HIC – individuals who work in ICU settings in LRS may have little experience with appropriate technologies and, conversely, providers in HIC with greater access to technologies may not have experience working in LRS. This reveals a potential unexplored frontier in addressing inequities in health care by developing equipment and technologies with high accessibility in areas of the world with the highest burdens of treatable pediatric disease. Based on this survey data, next steps may include expanding the survey to a larger audience representing LRS, generating appropriate funding streams for development efforts, and facilitating international discussion and training on this topic given varying levels of comfort and experience with the implementation of pediatric medical devices in LRS.
